segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By no means! We who died to sin—how can we still live in it?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We know this: our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, so that we would no longer be slaves to sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the one who has died has been justified from sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death is no longer his master.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So you too must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey the body’s desires,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and do not present the parts of your body to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as people alive from the dead, and the parts of your body to God as weapons of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For sin will not be your master, for you are not under law but under grace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God that, though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and, having been set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness, so now present the parts of your body as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So what fruit did you have then from the things you are now ashamed of? For the end of those things is death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, having been set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit, leading to holiness, and the end is eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the gracious gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.phrase: united with him in the likeness of his death
notes.traditional: planted together in the likeness of his death
notes.note: The Greek says only “we have become joined with the likeness of his death”; “with him” is supplied, as in most modern versions. The alternative is that believers are joined to the likeness itself, perhaps meaning baptism. The second half of the verse is compressed in Greek (“we will also be of the resurrection”), and the words carried over from the first half are filled in here.

Literally “our old human being.” After the contrast between Adam and Christ in the previous chapter, many interpreters take the phrase to mean the person one was as a member of Adam’s humanity, not merely a part of one’s inner psychology. “Self” is the usual modern rendering and is kept here.

The verb means to put something out of operation or deprive it of force; it is not the ordinary word for destroying. Translations are divided here between “destroyed,” “done away with” and “rendered powerless.” The last is chosen because Paul goes on to speak of the body as still present and still needing to be offered to God (verses 12–13).

Most versions have “freed” or “set free,” but the verb is Paul’s regular word for “justify,” that is, declare to be in the right or acquit; a different verb is used for “set free” in verses 18 and 22. The thought seems to be that death settles sin’s claim on a person, as a legal case closes when the defendant dies. Greek has a single word-family where English divides between “just/justify” and “righteous/righteousness,” so this verb belongs with “righteousness” later in the chapter.

The word can mean tools or implements in general, and most versions have “instruments.” In the usage of the period, and everywhere else in Paul, the plural means weapons or armor, and the surrounding language of reigning and mastery suits a military picture. Many commentators therefore prefer “weapons.”

notes.phrase: to which you were handed over
notes.traditional: which was delivered to you; to which you were committed
notes.note: One would expect teaching to be handed on to people, but Paul reverses it: the people were handed over to the teaching. The verb is the ordinary one for transferring someone into another’s control, and in this context it pictures slaves passing to a new master. Versions that render “committed” or “entrusted” soften that image.

The word can denote the process of being made holy (“sanctification”) or the resulting state of being set apart for God (“holiness”). English versions are divided, and the same word is rendered the same way in verse 22.

notes.phrase: from the things you are now ashamed of
notes.note: The verse can be punctuated differently: “So what fruit did you have then? Things of which you are now ashamed.” Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and both readings have scholarly support. The rendering here follows the punctuation of the edition translated, which implies the answer “none.”
The adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length.

The word was commonly used for a soldier’s pay or ration money, which fits the military imagery of verse 13. Sin is pictured as a commander or master who pays what is owed, and God as one who gives what is not earned.

The Greek word is formed from the word for “grace” used throughout this chapter, and a Greek reader would hear the connection. “Gracious gift” keeps that link; “gift” or “free gift” is the usual rendering.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the whole New Testament and translations split between “slave,” “servant” and “bondservant,” which changes how readers hear both social settings and metaphors like this one.
Versions vary between “sanctification,” “holiness” and “consecration” across Romans, 1 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians and Hebrews, and readers would not recognize it as one term.
Occurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, the Pastorals and 1 Peter with renderings ranging from “gift” and “free gift” to “spiritual gift,” and its link to χάρις is easily lost.
A central Pauline term rendered variously as “flesh,” “sinful nature,” “human nature” or “natural limitations,” where inconsistency hides the thread of Paul’s argument.
Key verb in Romans 4 and elsewhere, rendered “reckon,” “count,” “credit,” “consider” or “impute,” and readers should be able to see when the same accounting term recurs.
